raw_case_text:
A 47 year-old-man, human immunodeficiency virus negative, with a recent diagnosis of central nervous system lymphoma presented with perianal skin lesions and nonbloody diarrhea. The skin lesions began as nodules that progressed to a roughened plaque and in the minority, ulceration. The lesions began eight weeks prior to presentation, were multiple, scattered in the perianal area and upper thigh bilaterally, and three centimeters at the widest diameter (Figure 1). A more distinct lesion with irregular border was present over the sacrum consistent with a decubitus ulcer. The patient had been diagnosed with a CNS lymphoma six weeks prior to admission when he presented to another hospital with lower extremity weakness, saddle anesthesia, and fecal incontinence, and was found to have a L1-L2 intramedullary spinal mass. He had emergent surgical resection of the mass and was treated with high-dose dexamethasone and further radiation therapy. He was additionally found to have a right temporal lobe mass that was resected and pathology was consistent with a B-cell lymphoma with T-cell infiltration. He had no other significant past medical history or immunocompromising condition. The lower extremity weakness persisted and primarily confined him to bed. For ongoing fecal incontinence and the nonhealing sacral decubitus ulcer, he ultimately had a diverting colostomy. Two weeks prior to presentation, his bowel movements became more liquid in consistency and increased in frequency. He denied abdominal pain. The perianal skin lesions were not painful, but the initial loss of sensation from the compressive spinal mass had not recovered. He remained on a dexamethasone taper and was transferred to this hospital for further evaluation for chemotherapy. His complete blood count was notable for a normocytic anemia, and his liver function tests for an elevated alkaline phosphatase. An excisional biopsy of one of the skin lesions from the upper thigh was obtained and sent for pathological examination.
Sections of the pathological specimen revealed a dense neutrophilic crust with numerous bacteria distributed in varying sized aggregates, and the underlying epidermis was acanthotic with artefactual subepidermal clefting. However, the superficial dermis demonstrated a distinct perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, and the endothelial cells were markedly enlarged (Figure 2). Some endothelial cells contained magenta-colored nuclear inclusions consistent with cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection which was confirmed by a positive CMV immunostain (Figure 3). Stains with periodic acid-Schiff and for acid-fast bacilli were negative.
The patient was treated with intravenous ganciclovir at five mg/kg every twelve hours for 21 days followed by transition to valganciclovir. A serum CMV viral load was 16,400 copies/mL at treatment initiation and was undetectable after four weeks of treatment. The diarrhea resolved within two weeks, and the skin lesions had completely healed at the time of switch to valganciclovir. Based on pathological findings and response to treatment, the diagnosis of cutaneous CMV was made. The primary mode of pathogenesis was thought to be local inoculation from fecal shedding. The diarrhea appeared to be a manifestation of CMV colitis, but given the commitment to CMV treatment and the response to therapy, no further investigation was performed. Unfortunately, the patient later died secondary to complications of an intracranial hemorrhage at the site of the temporal lobe resection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old HIV-negative man with recently diagnosed central nervous system lymphoma presented with an 8-week history of perianal and bilateral upper thigh skin lesions and a 2-week history of nonbloody liquid diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Six weeks prior to transfer, the patient presented to an outside hospital with lower extremity weakness, saddle anesthesia, and fecal incontinence, where an L1-L2 intramedullary spinal mass and a right temporal lobe mass were resected (pathology: B-cell lymphoma with T-cell infiltration) and treated with high-dose dexamethasone and radiation therapy, plus a diverting colostomy for fecal incontinence and a sacral decubitus ulcer. Eight weeks prior to current presentation, painless nodules appeared in the perianal area and bilateral upper thighs that progressed to roughened plaques and ulcers up to 3 cm wide. Two weeks prior to presentation, his ostomy/bowel output became more liquid and frequent without abdominal pain while he remained on a dexamethasone taper.
subjective.past_medical_history: Central nervous system B-cell lymphoma (L1-L2 intramedullary spinal cord and right temporal lobe masses resected 6 weeks prior) treated with high-dose dexamethasone and radiation; paraparesis, saddle anesthesia, and fecal incontinence status post diverting colostomy; sacral decubitus ulcer; HIV-negative.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painless perianal and upper thigh nodular/ulcerated plaques, sacral decubitus ulcer, 2 weeks of nonbloody liquid diarrhea, persistent lower extremity weakness, and saddle anesthesia; negative for abdominal pain. Medication: oral dexamethasone taper.

objective.physical_examination: Multiple scattered roughened plaques and ulcers (up to 3 cm in diameter) in the perianal region and bilateral upper thighs, an irregular sacral decubitus ulcer, persistent paraparesis confining him to bed, and persistent perineal/saddle sensory loss.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed normocytic anemia; liver function tests showed elevated alkaline phosphatase; HIV testing negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Excisional skin biopsy of an upper thigh lesion demonstrated an acanthotic epidermis beneath a bacteria-laden neutrophilic crust, a superficial dermal perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, and markedly enlarged dermal endothelial cells containing magenta-colored intranuclear inclusions that stained positive on CMV immunohistochemistry (PAS and AFB stains negative). Quantitative serum CMV viral load at treatment initiation was 16,400 copies/mL (undetectable after 4 weeks of therapy).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cutaneous perianal/thigh cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (via local fecal inoculation prior to diverting colostomy) and probable CMV colitis in a dexamethasone-immunosuppressed CNS lymphoma patient, confirmed by enlarged dermal endothelial cells with magenta intranuclear inclusions, positive CMV immunohistochemistry on thigh skin biopsy, and serum CMV viral load of 16,400 copies/mL. Treated with intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg every 12 hours for 21 days) followed by oral valganciclovir, achieving resolution of diarrhea within 2 weeks, complete healing of cutaneous lesions by day 21, and an undetectable serum CMV viral load at 4 weeks; the patient later died from an intracranial hemorrhage at the prior temporal lobe resection site.
